name: revision_moves
description: The verbs of editing: named, repeatable operations a reviser performs on existing prose — cutting, compressing, expanding, reordering, splitting and merging, substituting — plus a diagnosis table pairing each measurable symptom the craft diagnostics report with the move that treats it.

cut_moves.name: cut the throat-clearing opener
cut_moves.definition: Delete the warm-up sentence or clause that announces the subject before the prose begins to say anything about it.
cut_moves.example: 'Before we can understand the settlement, it is worth considering its history. The history begins in 1974.' -> 'The history begins in 1974.'
cut_moves.effect: The paragraph starts at its first real assertion, and the reader stops paying an entrance fee.
cut_moves.caution: Some throat-clearing is orientation the reader needs; cut it only when the following sentence stands without it.

cut_moves.name: cut the last sentence of the paragraph
cut_moves.definition: Delete the closing sentence that restates, moralizes, or explains what the paragraph has already demonstrated.
cut_moves.example: '...the deposit cleared four days after the account was frozen. The timing, in other words, was not a coincidence.' -> stop at 'frozen.'
cut_moves.effect: Ends on the evidence rather than the gloss, and credits the reader with the inference.
cut_moves.caution: Keep it when the paragraph's point genuinely depends on an inference the reader cannot be expected to draw.

cut_moves.name: cut the first sentence of the paragraph
cut_moves.definition: Delete an abstract topic sentence and let the paragraph's second sentence — usually the concrete one — open it.
cut_moves.example: 'Enforcement was inconsistent. In 1998 the agency issued six fines; in 1999 it issued none.' -> 'In 1998 the agency issued six fines; in 1999 it issued none.'
cut_moves.effect: Replaces an assertion with a demonstration and converts the paragraph from a claim-plus-proof to a proof that implies its claim.

cut_moves.name: drop the frame
cut_moves.definition: Remove the framing matrix clause that reports the writer's relation to the content instead of the content.
cut_moves.example: 'What is interesting here is that the rule changed twice.' -> 'The rule changed twice.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes a layer of mediation; the fact arrives without a chaperone.

cut_moves.name: cut to the verb
cut_moves.definition: Delete everything before the sentence's real verb, promoting the buried predicate to the front of the clause.
cut_moves.example: 'One thing that should be noted about the second draft is that it removed the deadline.' -> 'The second draft removed the deadline.'
cut_moves.effect: Shortens the run-up to the action and puts a working verb where the reader is already looking for one.

cut_moves.name: cut the recap
cut_moves.definition: Delete the sentence or clause that summarizes material the reader finished a page ago.
cut_moves.example: 'As we saw in the previous section, the fund was insolvent. The trustees knew.' -> 'The trustees knew.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes redundancy and keeps forward motion; the connection survives without being narrated.
cut_moves.caution: In long-form nonfiction a single orienting clause after a chapter break earns its place.

cut_moves.name: cut the preview
cut_moves.definition: Delete the announcement of what the following passage will do.
cut_moves.example: 'This chapter will examine three failures of oversight.' -> begin with the first failure.
cut_moves.effect: Converts a table of contents into prose and saves the reader a paragraph of waiting.
cut_moves.caution: Technical and academic genres price previews as a service, not a fault; check the register before cutting.

cut_moves.name: cut the hedge stack
cut_moves.definition: Reduce a pile of stacked qualifiers to the single hedge that carries the real uncertainty.
cut_moves.example: 'It may perhaps be possible that the figure is roughly accurate.' -> 'The figure is roughly accurate.'
cut_moves.effect: Restores a stateable claim and makes the remaining hedge mean something.

cut_moves.name: cut the booster
cut_moves.definition: Delete the certainty intensifier and let the evidence supply the confidence.
cut_moves.example: 'This clearly and undeniably shows a pattern.' -> 'This shows a pattern.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes the sound of a writer arguing with an imagined doubter, which reads as weakness rather than force.

cut_moves.name: cut the second example
cut_moves.definition: Delete the confirming instance that adds no new dimension to the one already given.
cut_moves.example: Two anecdotes both showing a regulator missing a deadline -> keep the one with the checkable date.
cut_moves.effect: Keeps illustrative weight while halving the wordcount; the surviving example gains room for detail.
cut_moves.caution: Two examples are not redundant when the second establishes range rather than repetition.

cut_moves.name: cut the restated thesis
cut_moves.definition: Delete the reappearance of the book's thesis at the end of a section that has just proved something narrower.
cut_moves.example: '...which is why the audit failed. Once again, institutions protect themselves before they protect the public.' -> stop at 'failed.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes the machine-written cadence of thesis-evidence-thesis and lets sections accumulate instead of resetting.

cut_moves.name: cut the intensifier
cut_moves.definition: Delete very, really, extremely, incredibly, and their kin rather than upgrading the word they modify.
cut_moves.example: 'a very large loss' -> 'a large loss' or 'a $40 million loss'
cut_moves.effect: Either the noun was strong enough or it was not; the cut exposes which, and usually prompts a substitution.

cut_moves.name: cut the process narration
cut_moves.definition: Delete sentences that describe the writing rather than perform it.
cut_moves.example: 'Having established the timeline, we now turn to motive.' -> begin the motive paragraph.
cut_moves.effect: Removes scaffolding the reader was never meant to see; the section break already signals the turn.

cut_moves.name: cut the implied qualifier
cut_moves.definition: Delete a limiting phrase the sentence's own scope already carries.
cut_moves.example: 'In most cases, the deadline is typically thirty days.' -> 'The deadline is thirty days.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes a doubled apology for the same imprecision and shortens the distance to the fact.

cut_moves.name: cut one of the paired adjectives
cut_moves.definition: Where two coordinated modifiers cover nearly the same ground, delete the weaker one.
cut_moves.example: 'a slow and lumbering process' -> 'a lumbering process'
cut_moves.effect: Removes the doublet rhythm that makes prose sound padded, and forces the surviving adjective to be exact.

cut_moves.name: cut the explained joke
cut_moves.definition: Delete the clause that tells the reader why the preceding line is funny.
cut_moves.example: 'He filed it under Miscellaneous, which was, of course, where everything inconvenient went.' -> stop at 'Miscellaneous.'
cut_moves.effect: Restores the reader's discovery, which is the whole payment a joke offers.

cut_moves.name: cut the reader-address aside
cut_moves.definition: Delete the parenthetical turn to the reader that interrupts an argument to check whether it is landing.
cut_moves.example: 'The number is 4 percent (yes, you read that right).' -> 'The number is 4 percent.'
cut_moves.effect: Keeps the writer out of the reader's peripheral vision and lets the fact carry its own surprise.

cut_moves.name: cut the connective adverb
cut_moves.definition: Delete a sentence-initial however, moreover, furthermore, or additionally when the logical relation is already visible.
cut_moves.example: 'However, the second audit found nothing.' -> 'The second audit found nothing.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes the loudest machine-prose tell at the sentence opener and lets juxtaposition do the connecting.
cut_moves.caution: Genuine concession and contrast sometimes need the signal; cut the ones the sentence order already implies.

cut_moves.name: cut the redundant definition
cut_moves.definition: Delete a gloss of a term the reader has already been given, or one the context defines by use.
cut_moves.example: 'The escrow — an account held by a third party — was empty.' -> 'The escrow was empty.' (fourth mention)
cut_moves.effect: Saves the reader from being taught twice, which reads as condescension by the second time.

cut_moves.name: cut the contrast frame
cut_moves.definition: Delete the not-x-but-y or it-is-not-merely construction and assert y directly.
cut_moves.example: 'This is not just a story about money; it is a story about trust.' -> 'This is a story about trust.'
cut_moves.effect: Removes the single most detectable stock cadence in machine-assisted prose, and forces the claim to stand unaided.

cut_moves.name: cut the scene's arrival and departure
cut_moves.definition: Delete the character's approach to the room and exit from it; enter at the first consequential line, leave on the last.
cut_moves.example: 'She parked, walked up two flights, and knocked. He opened the door. "You lied to the board."' -> '"You lied to the board."'
cut_moves.effect: Compresses dead time and starts the scene where the pressure is.

cut_moves.name: cut the attributed obvious
cut_moves.definition: Delete an authority citation for a claim no informed reader disputes.
cut_moves.example: 'As Smith (2011) notes, incentives influence behavior.' -> 'Incentives influence behavior.'
cut_moves.effect: Reserves citation weight for claims that need it and stops the prose reading as a literature review.

cut_moves.name: cut the parenthetical
cut_moves.definition: Delete a bracketed aside, or promote it to a clause if it turns out to matter.
cut_moves.example: 'The rule (which had been amended in 2003) applied.' -> 'The rule applied.' or 'The 2003 amendment made the rule apply.'
cut_moves.effect: Forces a decision the parenthesis was postponing: the material is either load-bearing or it is not.

compression_moves.name: nominalization to verb
compression_moves.definition: Convert an abstract noun back into the verb it was made from, and give that verb its agent.
compression_moves.example: 'The implementation of the policy by the board occurred in March.' -> 'The board implemented the policy in March.'
compression_moves.effect: Cuts words, restores an actor, and turns a static clause into an event.

compression_moves.name: subordinate clause to participial phrase
compression_moves.definition: Recast a finite subordinate clause as a participial modifier attached to the main clause.
compression_moves.example: 'Because he had already signed the waiver, he could not sue.' -> 'Having signed the waiver, he could not sue.'
compression_moves.effect: Removes a conjunction and a finite verb, and hangs the circumstance on the main clause instead of beside it.
compression_moves.caution: Check the implied subject; a participle that attaches to the wrong noun dangles.

compression_moves.name: relative clause to appositive
compression_moves.definition: Strip the relative pronoun and copula so a defining clause becomes a renaming noun phrase.
compression_moves.example: 'Ruiz, who was the auditor on the account, resigned.' -> 'Ruiz, the auditor on the account, resigned.'
compression_moves.effect: Two words shorter and rhythmically lighter; the identification stops competing with the main verb.

compression_moves.name: relative clause to modifier
compression_moves.definition: Collapse a whole relative clause into a single premodifying adjective or noun.
compression_moves.example: 'a report that was produced internally' -> 'an internal report'
compression_moves.effect: Maximum compression at the noun phrase; keeps the sentence's weight on its verb.
compression_moves.caution: Premodifier stacks of three or more become bureaucratic; compress one clause, not three.

compression_moves.name: list to pair
compression_moves.definition: Cut a four- or five-item list to the two items that mark its range.
compression_moves.example: 'fines, warnings, suspensions, consent decrees, and referrals' -> 'fines and referrals'
compression_moves.effect: Preserves the span of the category while restoring sentence speed; the pair reads as a choice rather than an inventory.

compression_moves.name: list to triple
compression_moves.definition: Trim a long enumeration to three members ordered by increasing weight.
compression_moves.example: seven consequences -> the mildest, a middling one, and the one that ends the argument
compression_moves.effect: Recovers the tricolon's closure, which a six-item list dissipates.

compression_moves.name: appositive absorption
compression_moves.definition: Fold an appositive's content into the noun phrase it renames, removing the commas.
compression_moves.example: 'The chair, a former prosecutor, objected.' -> 'The former prosecutor in the chair objected.'
compression_moves.effect: Removes an interruption from a sentence that already has one, smoothing a stuttering middle.

compression_moves.name: sentence pair to semicolon
compression_moves.definition: Join two closely related sentences with a semicolon and delete the connective that linked them.
compression_moves.example: 'The first audit found nothing. However, the second found the missing invoices.' -> 'The first audit found nothing; the second found the missing invoices.'
compression_moves.effect: Puts the relation in the punctuation rather than in a word, and lets the parallel structure carry the contrast.

compression_moves.name: clause to absolute
compression_moves.definition: Reduce an accompanying-circumstance clause to a nominative absolute — noun plus participle, no conjunction.
compression_moves.example: 'While his hands were shaking, he signed it.' -> 'His hands shaking, he signed it.'
compression_moves.effect: Compresses and simultaneously varies the sentence opener, which is why it doubles as a monotony cure.

compression_moves.name: passive to active
compression_moves.definition: Restore the agent to subject position and drop the by-phrase and auxiliary.
compression_moves.example: 'The file was destroyed by the contractor.' -> 'The contractor destroyed the file.'
compression_moves.effect: Sheds two words and names who did it, which is usually the fact the passive was hiding.
compression_moves.caution: Keep the passive when the patient is the paragraph's topic or the agent is genuinely unknown.

compression_moves.name: expletive removal
compression_moves.definition: Delete a there-is or it-is opener and promote the real subject.
compression_moves.example: 'There are three reasons the deadline slipped.' -> 'The deadline slipped for three reasons.'
compression_moves.effect: Removes a dummy subject and a linking verb, converting an announcement into a statement.
compression_moves.caution: Existential there earns its place when the sentence's whole job is to introduce something new.

compression_moves.name: prepositional chain collapse
compression_moves.definition: Break a run of three or more stacked of/for/to phrases by turning one into a possessive or a verb.
compression_moves.example: 'the effect of the reduction of the size of the panel' -> 'shrinking the panel'
compression_moves.effect: Cuts the sentence's longest dead stretch and usually recovers a verb in the process.

compression_moves.name: phrase to word
compression_moves.definition: Replace a multi-word circumlocution with the single word it paraphrases.
compression_moves.example: 'in the event that' -> 'if'; 'at this point in time' -> 'now'; 'due to the fact that' -> 'because'
compression_moves.effect: The cheapest compression available and the one that most reliably lowers the register toward plain speech.

compression_moves.name: gap the repeated verb
compression_moves.definition: Delete a verb repeated across parallel clauses and let the structure supply it.
compression_moves.example: 'The first bid was rejected and the second bid was accepted.' -> 'The first bid was rejected, the second accepted.'
compression_moves.effect: Tightens the parallel and speeds the second member, so the contrast snaps.

compression_moves.name: quotation to paraphrase
compression_moves.definition: Replace a long block quotation with a compressed paraphrase, keeping only the phrase whose exact wording matters.
compression_moves.example: Six lines of a consent decree -> 'The decree required quarterly reports "in a form acceptable to the Commission."'
compression_moves.effect: Retains the evidentiary weight and the telling phrase while removing the reader's obligation to translate legalese.
compression_moves.caution: Paraphrase changes the record; keep the quotation whenever a reader might dispute your reading.

compression_moves.name: dialogue to summarized speech
compression_moves.definition: Convert a rendered exchange into narrated report where the content matters and the performance does not.
compression_moves.example: Two pages of negotiation -> 'They spent an hour arguing about the escrow and settled on sixty days.'
compression_moves.effect: Buys back pace and reserves rendered dialogue for the exchanges whose exact words carry the scene.

compression_moves.name: scene to summary
compression_moves.definition: Replace a dramatized sequence with a narrated compression of its outcome.
compression_moves.example: A rendered board meeting -> 'The board voted five to two, and the chair left before the minutes were signed.'
compression_moves.effect: Adjusts the pace of a chapter that dramatizes everything, and marks by contrast which scenes are worth full staging.

compression_moves.name: connective to juxtaposition
compression_moves.definition: Delete the logical connective and set the two statements side by side, letting parataxis assert the relation.
compression_moves.example: 'The fund was insolvent, and therefore the bonuses were paid out of new deposits.' -> 'The fund was insolvent. The bonuses came out of new deposits.'
compression_moves.effect: Shortens, hardens, and moves the inference to the reader, where it lands harder.

compression_moves.name: modifier into compound
compression_moves.definition: Convert a postmodifying phrase into a hyphenated premodifier.
compression_moves.example: 'a plan that lasts five years' -> 'a five-year plan'
compression_moves.effect: Compresses the noun phrase and keeps the sentence's stress on its predicate.

compression_moves.name: statistic compression
compression_moves.definition: Replace a sentence of statistical apparatus with the single number that carries the point.
compression_moves.example: 'Of the 412 filings reviewed, 37 were found to contain at least one omission, a rate of approximately 9 percent.' -> 'Nine percent of the 412 filings had omissions.'
compression_moves.effect: Keeps the checkable figures and drops the method narration into a note where it belongs.

compression_moves.name: delete the doubled agent
compression_moves.definition: When a clause names an actor and then re-describes that actor's function, keep one.
compression_moves.example: 'The committee, which was responsible for approving expenses, approved the expense.' -> 'The committee approved the expense.'
compression_moves.effect: Removes a tautological loop that makes prose feel like it is treading water.

expansion_moves.name: unpack the abstraction into a case
expansion_moves.definition: Replace or follow an abstract claim with one concrete instance carrying names, dates, and quantities.
expansion_moves.example: 'Oversight was weak.' -> 'The examiner assigned to the fund covered eleven other institutions and visited this one twice in six years.'
expansion_moves.effect: Converts a proposition the reader can only accept or reject into a scene the reader can check.

expansion_moves.name: add the missing step
expansion_moves.definition: Insert the inferential step the argument skipped between two adjacent claims.
expansion_moves.example: 'The rule changed, so the fines stopped.' -> add the sentence explaining that the new rule moved enforcement to a body without staff.
expansion_moves.effect: Closes a gap the writer crossed from knowledge and the reader cannot cross at all.

expansion_moves.name: slow the key moment
expansion_moves.definition: Expand the two or three sentences on which a chapter turns, adding beats, sensory detail, or clause-level delay.
expansion_moves.example: 'He signed it.' -> three sentences covering the pen, the date he wrote, and the pause before the second signature.
expansion_moves.effect: Matches textual duration to importance, which is how a reader learns what mattered.
expansion_moves.caution: Slowing a moment that does not carry weight is padding; expand only at the pivot.

expansion_moves.name: add the counterexample
expansion_moves.definition: Introduce the instance that does not fit, and say what it costs the claim.
expansion_moves.example: After four cases of regulatory capture, add the agency that resisted it and why.
expansion_moves.effect: Raises credibility more than another confirming case, and pre-empts the reader's strongest objection.

expansion_moves.name: add the particular
expansion_moves.definition: Attach a name, a date, a place, or a number to a sentence that currently has none.
expansion_moves.example: 'A senior official later resigned.' -> 'The deputy comptroller, Ellen Prewitt, resigned that November.'
expansion_moves.effect: Raises the density of checkable detail, the single most reliable difference between reported and generated prose.

expansion_moves.name: add the sensory detail
expansion_moves.definition: Insert one perceptual particular — sound, texture, smell, light — into a passage rendered entirely in summary.
expansion_moves.example: 'They met in the annex.' -> 'They met in the annex, where the radiator ran all summer.'
expansion_moves.effect: Anchors an abstract scene in a body and a place; one detail does more than three.
expansion_moves.caution: One particular per passage; a catalogue of sensations reads as a set dressing exercise.

expansion_moves.name: add the objection and answer it
expansion_moves.definition: State the strongest available objection in its own voice, then answer it on the page.
expansion_moves.example: 'A reader will say the numbers are inflation-adjusted differently. They are — and adjusting them the other way moves the total by 3 percent, not by an order of magnitude.'
expansion_moves.effect: Converts a reader's private resistance into a shared step of the argument.

expansion_moves.name: add the mechanism
expansion_moves.definition: Explain how the stated effect is produced, not merely that it occurs.
expansion_moves.example: 'The incentive distorted the ratings.' -> add the two sentences describing who paid whom, and when the fee was booked.
expansion_moves.effect: Turns a correlation into an account the reader can test against other cases.

expansion_moves.name: add the number
expansion_moves.definition: Supply the quantity behind a vague magnitude word.
expansion_moves.effect: Replaces an adjective the reader must take on trust with a fact the reader can weigh.

expansion_moves.name: restore the scene
expansion_moves.definition: Dramatize a moment the draft summarized, when the summary hides the decision the chapter is about.
expansion_moves.example: 'They eventually agreed to release the report.' -> render the meeting in which the last objection was withdrawn.
expansion_moves.effect: Puts the reader in the room for the turn, which summary can report but not stage.

expansion_moves.name: add the second beat
expansion_moves.definition: Give a one-exchange interaction a follow-up move, so it becomes an exchange rather than a statement.
expansion_moves.example: A question answered flatly -> the answer, a pause, and the speaker's correction of it.
expansion_moves.effect: Creates the small oscillation that makes an interaction feel live instead of transacted.

expansion_moves.name: state the stakes
expansion_moves.definition: Add the sentence naming what is lost if the situation goes the wrong way, and for whom.
expansion_moves.example: 'The audit was delayed.' -> 'The audit was delayed, and the fund took another eleven months of deposits.'
expansion_moves.effect: Gives a factual passage a reason to be read at speed rather than skimmed.

expansion_moves.name: restore the source's own words
expansion_moves.definition: Replace a paraphrase with the quotation where the original phrasing is the evidence.
expansion_moves.example: 'The memo warned of insolvency.' -> 'The memo called the fund "functionally insolvent as of the first quarter."'
expansion_moves.effect: Moves the claim from the writer's authority to the record's, which is where a contested claim belongs.

expansion_moves.name: add the limiting condition
expansion_moves.definition: Scope an overbroad claim by naming the conditions under which it holds.
expansion_moves.example: 'Regulators miss fraud.' -> 'Regulators staffed on a per-institution basis miss fraud that crosses institutions.'
expansion_moves.effect: Trades rhetorical reach for defensibility, and usually makes the claim more interesting.

expansion_moves.name: add the missing transition
expansion_moves.definition: Insert the sentence that names the relation between two paragraphs whose connection exists only in the writer's head.
expansion_moves.example: Between a chapter on staffing and one on fraud, add the sentence linking caseload to detection rate.
expansion_moves.effect: Repairs the most common structural complaint in review — 'I lost the thread' — at the lowest cost.

expansion_moves.name: voice the reader's question
expansion_moves.definition: Put the reader's likely objection or query on the page as a question, then answer it.
expansion_moves.example: 'Why did nobody call the police? Because the loss had not yet been booked, and nothing had formally gone missing.'
expansion_moves.effect: Converts confusion into structure and gives a flat expository stretch a two-part rhythm.
expansion_moves.caution: Two in a chapter is a device; six is a tic.

expansion_moves.name: dramatize the statistic
expansion_moves.definition: Follow a rate or total with a concrete equivalent the reader can picture.
expansion_moves.example: '2.4 million filings a year' -> 'about one filing every thirteen seconds of the working day'
expansion_moves.effect: Gives an unimaginable number a scale the reader's body understands.
expansion_moves.caution: The equivalent must be arithmetically honest; a vivid comparison that inflates is worse than the bare number.

expansion_moves.name: extend the metaphor one clause
expansion_moves.definition: Take a live figure one step further into its source domain rather than abandoning it after the noun.
expansion_moves.example: 'The agency was a sieve.' -> 'The agency was a sieve, and everyone knew which holes were the big ones.'
expansion_moves.effect: Converts decoration into thinking: the extension has to be true of the subject, so it does argumentative work.
expansion_moves.caution: One extension; a third clause turns the figure into an allegory the subject cannot support.

expansion_moves.name: add the aftermath
expansion_moves.definition: Follow a decisive event with the sentence showing what it cost afterward.
expansion_moves.example: 'The suit settled.' -> 'The suit settled, and the plaintiffs signed a clause forbidding them to describe the terms.'
expansion_moves.effect: Prevents the flat landing of a resolved passage and converts an outcome into a consequence.

reordering_moves.name: promote the buried lede
reordering_moves.definition: Move the most consequential sentence of a passage — usually found in the middle or at the end — to the front.
reordering_moves.example: A paragraph on committee procedure whose fourth sentence reports that the minutes were altered -> open on the alteration.
reordering_moves.effect: Aligns the reader's attention with the material's importance, and often makes the surrounding sentences cuttable.

reordering_moves.name: invert the paragraph
reordering_moves.definition: Move the paragraph's final sentence to the front and let the rest follow as support.
reordering_moves.example: A build-up ending in 'the deposits were never insured' -> begin there.
reordering_moves.effect: Converts a suspended paragraph into a thesis-first one; the fastest test of whether the suspense was earned.

reordering_moves.name: move the qualifier after the claim
reordering_moves.definition: Relocate a leading hedge or condition to the position after the assertion it limits.
reordering_moves.example: 'Although the data are incomplete, enforcement fell.' -> 'Enforcement fell, though the data are incomplete.'
reordering_moves.effect: The claim reaches the reader before its caveat, so the sentence asserts rather than apologizes.

reordering_moves.name: move the punch word last
reordering_moves.definition: Rearrange the clause so the word carrying the meaning takes the terminal position.
reordering_moves.example: 'The fund was insolvent by March, according to its own auditors.' -> 'By March, its own auditors called the fund insolvent.'
reordering_moves.effect: Puts the emphasis where English intonation already places it, which is why end-placed words are remembered.

reordering_moves.name: front the adverbial
reordering_moves.definition: Move a time, place, or manner adverbial to the head of the sentence.
reordering_moves.example: 'The board met again in November, after two postponements.' -> 'After two postponements, the board met again in November.'
reordering_moves.effect: Breaks a run of subject-first openers and sets the frame before the clause arrives.

reordering_moves.name: front an absolute
reordering_moves.definition: Open the sentence with a nominative absolute, delaying the subject.
reordering_moves.example: 'He signed with his hands shaking.' -> 'His hands shaking, he signed.'
reordering_moves.effect: Varies the opener class and adds a second observed detail without adding a sentence.

reordering_moves.name: cleft the sentence
reordering_moves.definition: Recast as an it-cleft or wh-cleft to force a specific element into focus.
reordering_moves.example: 'The auditors reported it in March.' -> 'It was the auditors, not the trustees, who reported it.'
reordering_moves.effect: Explicitly marks contrast where a plain clause leaves the emphasis ambiguous.
reordering_moves.caution: Clefts are heavy; one per page, at the sentence whose emphasis actually matters.

reordering_moves.name: reorder the list by weight
reordering_moves.definition: Sort a series so the members ascend in force, with the heaviest last.
reordering_moves.example: 'fines, criminal referrals, and warning letters' -> 'warning letters, fines, and criminal referrals'
reordering_moves.effect: Gives the series a climax rather than a random tail, which is what makes a list feel deliberate.

reordering_moves.name: move the example before the claim
reordering_moves.definition: Lead with the instance and let the generalization follow it.
reordering_moves.example: 'Capture is common. Consider the examiner who...' -> 'The examiner covering eleven institutions visited this one twice in six years. Capture rarely looks like corruption.'
reordering_moves.effect: Turns an assertion the reader must trust into a conclusion the reader has already begun to draw.

reordering_moves.name: move the definition to first use
reordering_moves.definition: Relocate a term's gloss from wherever it landed to the term's first appearance.
reordering_moves.example: A definition of 'consent decree' in chapter four moved to its first mention in chapter one.
reordering_moves.effect: Removes the stretch of prose the reader spent guessing, and the later definition's insult.

reordering_moves.name: repair given-new order
reordering_moves.definition: Rearrange a sentence so known information sits at the front and new information at the end.
reordering_moves.example: 'A second, unreported account held the missing funds.' (after a paragraph about the funds) -> 'The missing funds sat in a second account nobody had reported.'
reordering_moves.effect: Restores the topic chain across sentences; violated given-new order is what 'choppy' usually means.

reordering_moves.name: move the objection earlier
reordering_moves.definition: Relocate an anticipated counterargument from a late section to the point where the reader first thinks of it.
reordering_moves.example: A methodological caveat in the final section moved to the paragraph introducing the dataset.
reordering_moves.effect: Stops the reader arguing with the page for twenty paragraphs; concessions cost less the sooner they are made.

reordering_moves.name: delay the thesis
reordering_moves.definition: Move the governing claim from the opening to a position after the evidence that earns it.
reordering_moves.example: A section opening on 'regulators protect institutions, not depositors' -> the same sentence at the section's end.
reordering_moves.effect: Lets the reader arrive at the conclusion rather than being handed it, which raises assent on contested claims.
reordering_moves.caution: Delay costs orientation; readers of technical and business genres expect the claim first.

reordering_moves.name: move the caveat out of the middle
reordering_moves.definition: Relocate a limiting clause that interrupts a sentence's spine to the head or tail of the sentence.
reordering_moves.example: 'The fund, though the trustees disputed this until 2009, was insolvent.' -> 'The fund was insolvent. The trustees disputed this until 2009.'
reordering_moves.effect: Restores the clause's momentum; interruptions belong where they cost least, not where they occurred to the writer.

reordering_moves.name: put the strongest evidence last
reordering_moves.definition: Reorder a section's evidence so the most decisive item closes it.
reordering_moves.example: Three documents ordered by discovery date -> ordered by force, with the signed memo last.
reordering_moves.effect: Ends on the reader's peak conviction rather than on whatever the research turned up most recently.

reordering_moves.name: front the time marker
reordering_moves.definition: Move a date or duration to the sentence's opening slot when the passage is a chronology.
reordering_moves.example: 'The bank failed in the third week of October, after two rescue attempts.' -> 'In the third week of October, after two rescue attempts, the bank failed.'
reordering_moves.effect: Makes a sequence readable as a sequence and varies openers in a passage that would otherwise be all subject-first.

reordering_moves.name: restore chronological order
reordering_moves.definition: Rewrite a paragraph that jumps backward and forward so events run in the order they happened.
reordering_moves.example: A paragraph reporting a resignation, then its cause, then its aftermath, then its date -> straight through from the cause.
reordering_moves.effect: Removes the reader's reconstruction work in passages where the sequence is the point rather than the device.
reordering_moves.caution: Only where the disorder is accidental; deliberate anachrony is a technique, not a defect.

reordering_moves.name: move the topic sentence to the end
reordering_moves.definition: Shift a paragraph's governing sentence from the first position to the last.
reordering_moves.example: 'Enforcement varied by region. In 1998... In 2001...' -> the regional variation stated after the two figures.
reordering_moves.effect: Varies paragraph architecture in a chapter where every paragraph opens on its claim, the commonest structural monotony.

reordering_moves.name: hoist the shared element
reordering_moves.definition: Factor a repeated word or phrase out of parallel clauses and state it once at the front.
reordering_moves.example: 'The board approved the loan, the board approved the waiver, the board approved the extension.' -> 'The board approved the loan, the waiver, and the extension.'
reordering_moves.effect: Shortens and sharpens the parallel; the repetition survives as structure instead of as words.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the run-on
splitting_and_merging.definition: Break a sentence carrying two independent assertions into two sentences.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'The examiner filed no report and the fund went on taking deposits for another year, which nobody flagged.' -> three sentences.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Recovers a stress position for each claim and raises burstiness where every sentence has drifted long.

splitting_and_merging.name: split at the second subordinator
splitting_and_merging.definition: Cut a long sentence at its second subordinating conjunction and promote what follows to its own sentence.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'Because X, the board, which had already Y, decided Z, although W.' -> two sentences, the concession standing alone.
splitting_and_merging.effect: A mechanical rule for a sentence you know is too long but cannot see where to break.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the paragraph at the turn
splitting_and_merging.definition: Break a paragraph where its subject or its stance changes, even mid-argument.
splitting_and_merging.example: A paragraph on the audit's findings that becomes a paragraph on the trustees' response -> two.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Gives the second movement its own opening position and restores paragraph-length variation.

splitting_and_merging.name: split on the semicolon
splitting_and_merging.definition: Replace a semicolon with a period when the two halves are doing separate work.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'The report was never filed; the deadline had passed six weeks earlier.' -> two sentences.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Hardens the join; a period asserts twice where a semicolon asserts once with an aside.

splitting_and_merging.name: merge the thin paragraphs
splitting_and_merging.definition: Combine consecutive short paragraphs that develop one idea into a single paragraph.
splitting_and_merging.example: Three two-sentence paragraphs on the same meeting -> one paragraph of six sentences.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Removes the fragmented, listicle rhythm of prose broken by reflex rather than by structure.

splitting_and_merging.name: absorb the fragment
splitting_and_merging.definition: Fold a sentence fragment into the sentence before it, or promote it to a full clause.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'The audit found nothing. Or almost nothing.' -> 'The audit found almost nothing.'
splitting_and_merging.effect: Forces a judgment about whether the fragment was an effect or an accident; kept fragments become deliberate.
splitting_and_merging.caution: Fragments are a legitimate rhythmic device — this move is for the ones that recur unnoticed.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the section
splitting_and_merging.definition: Divide an overlong section at its internal hinge and give each half its own heading.
splitting_and_merging.example: A twelve-page section covering both detection and response -> two sections.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Makes the structure navigable and exposes whether the second half was ever properly argued.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the chapter at the false ending
splitting_and_merging.definition: Where a chapter reaches a natural close and then continues, cut it there and make the remainder a chapter.
splitting_and_merging.example: A chapter that resolves the investigation and then opens the trial -> two chapters.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Recovers a chapter ending the reader can feel, and gives the trailing material a proper opening.

splitting_and_merging.name: merge the near-duplicates
splitting_and_merging.definition: Combine two passages that make the same point in different words, keeping the better sentences from each.
splitting_and_merging.example: The same explanation of the escrow mechanism in chapters two and five -> one full treatment, one back-reference.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Removes the repetition that cross-chapter checks catch and parallel drafting causes.
splitting_and_merging.caution: Deliberate restatement across a long book is orientation; merge only what a reader would experience as déjà vu.

splitting_and_merging.name: break the wall of text
splitting_and_merging.definition: Split a page-long paragraph at its two strongest internal boundaries.
splitting_and_merging.example: One 400-word paragraph -> three paragraphs of roughly 130 words.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Restores white space and forces each fragment to declare a topic, which usually reveals a missing one.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the compound claim
splitting_and_merging.definition: Separate a sentence that asserts two things at once into its component claims, so each can be supported.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'The rule was ineffective and politically motivated.' -> two claims, two paragraphs, two kinds of evidence.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Exposes the half of the claim the draft never proved.

splitting_and_merging.name: merge the redundant list items
splitting_and_merging.definition: Collapse enumeration members that name the same thing at different levels of abstraction.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Turns a padded list into a real taxonomy, and often shortens three items to one.

splitting_and_merging.name: split the speech into two turns
splitting_and_merging.definition: Break a long speech with an action beat, an interruption, or the other party's line.
splitting_and_merging.example: A twelve-line speech -> six lines, the listener looking away, then the rest.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Restores the pressure of a two-party scene and prevents the monologue-in-quotes effect.

splitting_and_merging.name: merge into a periodic sentence
splitting_and_merging.definition: Fuse a sequence of short sentences into one suspended sentence whose main clause arrives last.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'The reports were late. The staff had quit. The board met anyway.' -> 'With the reports late and the staff gone, the board met anyway.'
splitting_and_merging.effect: Provides the long member a burstiness-flat passage needs, and subordinates detail to outcome.

splitting_and_merging.name: isolate the short paragraph
splitting_and_merging.definition: Split a passage so its single most important sentence stands alone as a one-sentence paragraph.
splitting_and_merging.example: 'Nobody read it for nine years.' set alone after a long expository paragraph.
splitting_and_merging.effect: Buys maximum emphasis with no new words; the rarest formatting move in a draft is the loudest.
splitting_and_merging.caution: Once or twice a chapter. Repeated, it becomes the thriller-blog rhythm.

substitution_moves.name: swap the example's domain
substitution_moves.definition: Replace an illustration with an equivalent one drawn from a different field, era, or scale.
substitution_moves.example: A software-outage analogy for a regulatory failure -> the same structure told through a hospital's on-call roster.
substitution_moves.effect: Breaks a chapter's habit of drawing every case from one world and reaches readers the first domain excluded.

substitution_moves.name: trade the adjective for a fact
substitution_moves.definition: Replace an evaluative modifier with the observation that produced the evaluation.
substitution_moves.example: 'a shocking delay' -> 'a delay of nineteen months'
substitution_moves.effect: Moves the judgment from the writer to the reader, where it is believed.

substitution_moves.name: swap the abstraction for the concrete noun
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a category noun with the physical thing it names in this instance.
substitution_moves.effect: Gives the sentence something the reader can see, and usually removes a hedge along with it.

substitution_moves.name: swap Latinate for Germanic
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a Latinate word with its short Anglo-Saxon equivalent, especially at the verb.
substitution_moves.effect: Lowers the register toward speech and shortens the sentence's rhythmic units.
substitution_moves.caution: The Latinate word sometimes carries a distinction the Germanic one loses; substitute for tone, not reflexively.

substitution_moves.name: adverb to verb
substitution_moves.definition: Delete an -ly adverb by choosing a verb that already contains it.
substitution_moves.effect: One word does two words' work, and the sentence loses the adverbial padding detectors count.

substitution_moves.name: simile to metaphor
substitution_moves.definition: Remove the like or as and assert the identity.
substitution_moves.example: 'The office ran like a machine that nobody maintained.' -> 'The office was a machine nobody maintained.'
substitution_moves.effect: Removes the softening comparison marker; the claim gets closer to the thing.

substitution_moves.name: swap the dead metaphor for a live one
substitution_moves.definition: Replace an exhausted figure with one drawn from the subject's own working world.
substitution_moves.example: 'a perfect storm of failures' -> a figure taken from the fund's own accounting: 'every entry booked twice and reconciled once'
substitution_moves.effect: Kills a stock phrase and produces an image only this subject could generate.

substitution_moves.name: quantifier to number
substitution_moves.definition: Replace many, several, most, or a majority with the count.
substitution_moves.example: 'many of the filings' -> 'thirty-one of the forty-four filings'
substitution_moves.effect: Removes a rhetorical smear from an empirical claim and lets the reader judge the magnitude.

substitution_moves.name: label to behavior
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a character or institutional label with the action that earns it.
substitution_moves.example: 'a careless administrator' -> 'an administrator who signed the forms without opening the file'
substitution_moves.effect: Shows instead of asserting, at almost no extra length.

substitution_moves.name: tag to action beat
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a dialogue attribution with a physical action that identifies the speaker.
substitution_moves.example: '"I signed it," he admitted reluctantly.' -> 'He turned the page back over. "I signed it."'
substitution_moves.effect: Removes an adverb and an editorializing verb while adding staging.

substitution_moves.name: upgrade the source
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a weak citation with the primary or better-credentialed source that supports the same claim.
substitution_moves.example: A trade-press summary -> the filed complaint it summarized.
substitution_moves.effect: Raises the claim's survivability under fact-check without changing a word of the prose around it.

substitution_moves.name: hedge to stated uncertainty
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a vague qualifier with the actual bound, range, or confidence.
substitution_moves.effect: Turns hedging into information; the sentence gets both more honest and more useful.

substitution_moves.name: second person to case
substitution_moves.definition: Replace an addressed hypothetical with a named instance.
substitution_moves.example: 'Imagine you are the examiner with eleven institutions.' -> 'The examiner had eleven institutions.'
substitution_moves.effect: Removes a reader-management device that dates quickly and substitutes evidence for invitation.

substitution_moves.name: pronoun to name
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a pronoun whose antecedent is more than a sentence away, or ambiguous between two candidates.
substitution_moves.example: 'He told him he had signed it.' -> 'Ruiz told the chair that Ruiz had signed it.', then rewrite for grace.
substitution_moves.effect: Removes the most common source of re-reading in a passage with two same-gender actors.

substitution_moves.name: negative to positive statement
substitution_moves.definition: Rewrite a not-construction as the affirmative claim it implies.
substitution_moves.example: 'The board did not approve the extension.' -> 'The board rejected the extension.'
substitution_moves.effect: Shorter, faster to parse, and forces the writer to state what happened rather than what did not.
substitution_moves.caution: Some negations are exact — 'did not approve' and 'rejected' differ when the board simply never voted.

substitution_moves.name: abstract subject to human agent
substitution_moves.definition: Replace an institutional or abstract grammatical subject with the person who acted.
substitution_moves.example: 'Policy considerations led to the delay.' -> 'The deputy comptroller delayed it.'
substitution_moves.effect: Restores accountability to the syntax, which in institutional subjects is usually the missing fact.
substitution_moves.caution: Do not invent an agent the record does not support; if the actor is genuinely unknown, say so.

substitution_moves.name: sharpen the connective
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a weak and or a vague this with the connective naming the actual relation.
substitution_moves.example: 'The rule changed and enforcement fell.' -> 'Enforcement fell because the rule moved it to an unstaffed office.'
substitution_moves.effect: States a relation the reader was left to guess, and usually exposes whether the writer knows it.

substitution_moves.name: stock phrase to plain words
substitution_moves.definition: Replace a set phrase, cliché, or house idiom with literal language.
substitution_moves.example: 'at the end of the day' -> 'finally'; 'a delicate balance' -> the two things being traded off, named
substitution_moves.effect: Removes the phrases slop audits count and forces a specific statement where a placeholder sat.

substitution_moves.name: re-register the sentence
substitution_moves.definition: Raise or lower a sentence's diction deliberately to break a passage of unvarying formality.
substitution_moves.example: In a formal paragraph: 'The reconciliation was never performed.' -> 'Nobody ever checked.'
substitution_moves.effect: Produces the register drop that reads as a human decision, and lands hardest at a paragraph's end.
substitution_moves.caution: One drop per passage; repeated register-switching reads as inconsistency rather than emphasis.

diagnosis_to_move.name: high subject-first share -> front an absolute or adverbial
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When most sentences open on their grammatical subject, vary the opener class rather than the opening word.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: construction_variety.py: subject-first share above the 85 percent default, or a run of three or more subject-first openers.
diagnosis_to_move.example: 'He signed the waiver.' -> 'His hands shaking, he signed the waiver.'
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Raises opener diversity in the way the metric is actually measuring, instead of pasting connectives at the front.
diagnosis_to_move.caution: Subject-first is the unmarked English order; the target is a run break, not a low share.

diagnosis_to_move.name: low burstiness -> pair a long sentence with a very short one
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When sentence lengths cluster around the mean, place a five-word sentence directly after a thirty-word one.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: cv below 0.45.
diagnosis_to_move.example: A paragraph of five 22-word sentences -> the fourth cut to 'Nobody checked.'
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Moves the variation metric by changing the contour, which is what burstiness measures, rather than by adding words.

diagnosis_to_move.name: low lexical diversity -> substitute at the repeated head noun
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When type-token measures fall, replace the recurring topic noun and its collocates rather than editing at random.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: mtld or mattr below band; vocab_variety.py overuse rows.
diagnosis_to_move.example: Six sentences on 'the process' -> 'the review', 'the sign-off', 'the eleven-day wait'.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Targets the actual source of low diversity: one abstraction reused where several concrete nouns belong.

diagnosis_to_move.name: uniform paragraph length -> split one and merge two
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When every paragraph is the same size, break the longest at its turn and combine two adjacent thin ones.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: para-cv below 0.30.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Restores paragraph-length variation, the layout-level version of burstiness and a documented machine-prose tell.

diagnosis_to_move.name: high adverb share -> adverb to verb across the passage
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When -ly adverbs run above the band, sweep the passage converting adverb-plus-weak-verb pairs into single strong verbs.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: adv% above 2.5.
diagnosis_to_move.example: 'moved quickly to formally reject' -> 'rushed to reject'
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Cuts the count and strengthens the verbs in one pass rather than deleting adverbs and leaving limp predicates.

diagnosis_to_move.name: low specificity -> add the particular
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When checkable detail per hundred words is thin, attach a name, date, or figure to the passage's assertions.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: spec (digits plus mid-sentence proper nouns per 100 words) below the corpus band.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Raises the density of verifiable particulars, which reads as reporting rather than generation.

diagnosis_to_move.name: opener run -> vary the opener class, not the first word
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When consecutive sentences share an opener type, change the grammatical shape rather than swapping one connective for another.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: construction_variety.py run detection, or check_prose.py opener-run.
diagnosis_to_move.example: 'However, ... Instead, ... Later, ...' all read as one run -> replace the second with a fronted participial phrase.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Fixes what the reader hears, which is the repeated shape, not the repeated word.

diagnosis_to_move.name: high nominalization rate -> nominalization to verb across the paragraph
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When buried verbs run high, convert the abstract nouns back to verbs and supply their agents paragraph by paragraph.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: register_report.py: nomin per 1000 words above the profile ceiling.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Lowers the metric and restores actors at the same time; the two defects always travel together.

diagnosis_to_move.name: high Latinate ratio -> swap Latinate for Germanic at the verb
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When the Latinate share exceeds the profile target, substitute at the verbs first and leave technical nouns alone.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: register_report.py: latin ratio above the profile maximum.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Moves the ratio where the reader feels it while preserving the precision that Latinate terminology carries.

diagnosis_to_move.name: hedge density -> cut the hedge stack and state the confidence
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When tentative markers run high, keep one hedge per claim and convert the rest to a stated bound.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: register_report.py: hedge per 1000 above the profile ceiling.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Reduces the count and improves the epistemics, rather than deleting hedges the claim needed.

diagnosis_to_move.name: booster density -> cut the booster and add the evidence
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When certainty markers run high, delete them and supply the fact that justified the confidence.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: register_report.py: boost per 1000 above the profile ceiling.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Trades assertion for proof; boosters cluster exactly where support is missing.

diagnosis_to_move.name: zero contractions -> lower the register in asides and speech
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When a draft has no contractions at all, introduce them first in dialogue and parenthetical asides rather than uniformly.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: register_report.py: contr rate at or near zero against a profile minimum.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Fixes the loudest formality signal in English prose without flattening a genuinely formal expository voice.

diagnosis_to_move.name: low compression ratio -> cut the repeated frame
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When a passage compresses unusually well, find the recurring sentence frame driving the redundancy and vary or delete it.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: prose_metrics.py: comp below band; slop_audit.py paragraph compression-ratio z-outliers.
diagnosis_to_move.example: Four paragraphs opening 'What makes this significant is that...' -> three of them recast.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Attacks the structural repetition the metric detects, which word-level substitution will not move.

diagnosis_to_move.name: monotone cadence -> change the final word
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When sentence endings concentrate in one stress shape, rewrite the tails so stressed monosyllables and trailing polysyllables alternate.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: rhythm_audit.py: one cadence label (trailing, falling, punch) dominating a chapter's endings.
diagnosis_to_move.example: '...was unnecessary. ...was contradictory. ...was extraordinary.' -> end one on 'it broke.'
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Restores the audible variety a reader registers as rhythm without touching sentence length.

diagnosis_to_move.name: no figures detected -> plant one scheme per section
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When a chapter shows almost no repetition, balance, or omission figures, place a single deliberate scheme at each section's strongest sentence.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: figure_detector.py: near-zero density across anaphora, tricolon, isocolon, asyndeton.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Adds patterned emphasis at the points that carry weight, instead of dusting figures across the chapter.
diagnosis_to_move.caution: Figure density is not a virtue in itself; the target is one or two placed well.

diagnosis_to_move.name: figure clumping -> redistribute the figures
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When detected figures concentrate in one chapter or one page, move or cut some and place others where the prose is bare.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: figure_detector.py distribution report: all hits in one unit.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Evens out the texture; clumping usually marks the passage the writer enjoyed writing rather than the one that mattered.

diagnosis_to_move.name: flat tension curve -> raise the stakes at the midpoint
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When a chapter's valence and tension rows both sit flat, insert or promote a consequence at the chapter's middle.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: arc_profiler.py: no movement in either row across the chapter's windows.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Gives a chapter a shape; flatness in both rows is the one arc finding worth acting on directly.

diagnosis_to_move.name: unpaid promise -> pay it or cut the promise
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When the ledger shows a question, forward reference, or introduced term with no downstream payoff, either deliver the payoff or delete the setup.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: setup_payoff.py rows with status unpaid or uncertain.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Closes the reader's open loops, which is what makes a long argument feel finished rather than abandoned.
diagnosis_to_move.caution: An unpaid question can be deliberate; the move is to make the choice, not to close every loop.

diagnosis_to_move.name: near-duplicate paragraphs -> merge and differentiate
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When two passages score as near-duplicates, merge them into one full treatment and leave a back-reference at the second site.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: find_near_duplicates.py cross-chapter matches; check_repetition.py hits.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Removes the repetition parallel drafting produces and recovers the space for the material the second pass should have added.

diagnosis_to_move.name: slop vocabulary density -> stock phrase to plain words
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When stock-vocabulary density runs high, replace each flagged phrase with a literal statement rather than a synonym.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: slop_audit.py quantitative pass: slop-vocabulary density at file or paragraph level.
diagnosis_to_move.example: 'a testament to' -> the evidence itself; 'navigate the complexities of' -> the specific difficulty, named
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Synonym substitution moves the phrase off the list and leaves the emptiness; literal statement removes both.

diagnosis_to_move.name: contrast-frame rate -> cut the contrast frame
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When not-x-but-y and its kin recur, rewrite each as a direct assertion and keep at most one in a chapter.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: slop_audit.py: contrast-frame rate above the corpus norm.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Removes the most recognizable machine cadence at the sentence level, which no amount of vocabulary work will hide.

diagnosis_to_move.name: thesis restatement -> cut the restated thesis
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When sections end by restating the book's argument, delete the restatement and end on the section's own last fact.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: slop_audit.py LLM judge: thesis-restatement tell firing across multiple sections.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Breaks the claim-evidence-claim loop that makes chapters feel interchangeable.

diagnosis_to_move.name: high detector window score -> rewrite the flagged window by hand
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When the AI-detector cross-check flags a window, rewrite that specific passage manually rather than re-prompting the whole chapter.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: pangram_check.py: elevated windows[].ai_assistance_score. Read fraction_ai as a one-bit verdict, never as a score.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Concentrates effort on the passage that actually scored, and keeps the rest of the chapter's voice intact.
diagnosis_to_move.caution: The detector signal is advisory and window-local; a flagged window is a place to look, not a verdict on the chapter.

diagnosis_to_move.name: missing discourse-move coverage -> add the absent move
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When the move profile lacks a family the genre expects — concession, counterargument, example — write the missing move into the section that needed it.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: move_annotator.py coverage audit against the genre profile.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Fixes a structural gap rather than a surface one; missing concession moves are why arguments read as brittle.

diagnosis_to_move.name: very-long band spike -> split at the second subordinator
diagnosis_to_move.definition: When the very-long band carries an unusual share of sentences, break each offender mechanically at its second subordinator.
diagnosis_to_move.symptom: construction_variety.py: elevated share in the 36-plus-word length band.
diagnosis_to_move.effect: Reduces the band and raises burstiness in one pass, with a rule that does not require rereading the argument.
